name: Yara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Yara, thanks for doing this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a refrigerated 12-tonne truck for a food wholesaler, delivering to restaurants, cafés and a couple of hotel kitchens in the city. I'm out by five, I do about fourteen drops, and every one is different: a back alley, a basement hatch, a chef who wants the fish before the veg. I like that it's a puzzle. What wears me out is parking, honestly, and the traffic wardens.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in the job, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. I ask it to reorder my drops when a road's closed, I get it to translate notes from the kitchen porters, and I used it to set up my investments. I share a flat with my cousin Dina, no partner right now. I've got about ten months of pay saved and some money in an index fund, which is like a basket of shares that just follows the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got oversold. I'd still be telling people at the depot to use it for the boring stuff, like checking invoices against what's on the pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much changes for me, and that's fine. Plenty of wholesalers are hiring chilled drivers, so I could move tomorrow if I wanted. I'd keep doing what I do and keep growing the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep putting a few hundred a month into the index fund. I'd show a couple of the older drivers how to use the AI on their phones for the paperwork. And I'd probably go for my artic licence next year, just because the pay is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I like it when things move. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a bit flat'. Would you want more change than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, yes. I like new stuff. I got bored once on a job that never changed and I left after eight months. In the plateau world I'd probably make my own change, like the artic licence, just to keep it interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you show the AI tools to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, who's been driving for the wholesaler for thirty years. He spends twenty minutes after every shift fighting with the delivery paperwork. I showed him once how to photograph a note and have it filled in, and he looked at me like I'd done a magic trick.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** that got oversold.
I'd keep telling depot drivers to use it for **boring paperwork**.
think: I think **not much changes** for me, and that's fine.
With **plenty of chilled jobs** around, I could move tomorrow if I wanted.
do: Keep driving and add **a few hundred** a month to the index fund.
Show **older drivers** how to use AI for delivery paperwork.
Go for my **artic licence** next year for better pay.
feel: She feels **calm** but a little bored, since she enjoys change.
S0.quote: I got bored once on a job that never changed and I left after eight months.
fieldNote: She treats stability as **slightly dull**, and would create her own change.
She acts as an informal **AI helper** for older colleagues.
Her savings and **local demand** for drivers make this world feel low risk.

steps.text: Add a few hundred a month to her index fund
Take the articulated lorry licence test next year
Keep driving the chilled restaurant round for the wholesaler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for people who get on board early. If the ordering and the route planning go to software, drivers like me who already use it will be the ones who make it work on the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job changes a lot more than it shrinks. My bit of the job is the alleys and the basement hatches, and robots are slow in this picture. The people I'd watch are the ones in the order office, because restaurants will just talk to an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager if I can be the driver who tests the new planning software, and write up what goes wrong. I'd keep saving and investing at the same rate. And I'd start a short online course in logistics planning, because if the jobs move from desks to checking the software, I want to be the one checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest. This is the kind of change I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the order office would feel it. Does that worry you for anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Marisol, who takes the chef orders. She's the reason my runs work, because she knows which kitchen will be shut on a Monday. If an app replaces her, I'd lose all that. I'd try to get her to write it down so the software actually learns it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My cousin Dina says I always assume I'll be the one who lands on my feet. She's probably right. But I've got ten months of savings and a licence that's in demand, so I can afford to be a bit relaxed.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for drivers who get on board early.
I'd say drivers who use the software will **make it work** on the road.
think: I think my job **changes more** than it shrinks because alleys and hatches stay hands-on.
I'd worry for the **order office**, especially the person who knows every kitchen.
do: Volunteer to **test the planning software** and report what goes wrong.
Start a short **online logistics course** to check software plans.
Keep **saving and investing** at the same rate.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little excited by change she enjoys.
S1.quote: My cousin Dina says I always assume I'll be the one who lands on my feet.
fieldNote: She sees herself as the **bridge** between software and the road.
She's honest about **possible overconfidence**, backed by real savings.
She wants a colleague's **local knowledge** captured, not lost, when the order desk is automated.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the wholesaler's new route-planning software
Take a short online course in logistics planning
Keep adding the same monthly amount to her index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change of our lives and anyone who says they're ready is lying. I'd tell people to act now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my driving job probably ends around 2031, when robots can do the drops. The thinking jobs in logistics go even sooner, in 2028, so I can't just hop to a planning desk either. Even my clever little plan to be the software checker doesn't last long in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look hard for jobs that sit between the machines and people, like supervising a fleet of driverless trucks from a control room, or fixing the refrigeration units on them. I'd start a course in refrigeration engineering straight away, because cold chain kit breaks a lot. I'd move a chunk of savings into the index fund, because if AI makes companies richer, I want a piece of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an awake way, not a frozen way. It's scary and I'd still rather be busy than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put more money into shares. What if that goes wrong too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost some money, but I'd still have six months in cash. I'd never put the emergency money in. If everyone's work gets cheaper, the owners win, so I'd rather be a tiny owner than only a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. In 2028 the office jobs go, but I can still drive until about 2031. So I'd earn while I study, finish a refrigeration ticket by 2030, and be fixing the trucks before they stop needing a driver.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest change** of our lives and nobody is truly ready.
I'd tell people to **act now**, not in 2030.
think: I think my **driving job ends** around 2031 when robots can do drops.
Planning desks go in 2028, so my **software-checker plan** fails too.
do: Start a **refrigeration engineering** course straight away.
Apply for **control-room jobs** supervising driverless truck fleets.
Move part of my savings into **the index fund**, keeping six months in cash.
feel: She feels **anxious** but energised, preferring action to waiting.
S2.quote: If everyone's work gets cheaper, the owners win, so I'd rather be a tiny owner than only a worker.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year robot gap** as a study window while still earning.
Her money logic is **ownership**: invest in the firms gaining from AI.
She protects a **cash floor** of six months even while taking risks.

steps.text: Enrol in a refrigeration engineering course straight away
Apply for control-room jobs supervising driverless truck fleets
Move part of her savings into the index fund, keeping six months' cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get it right, so let's not waste them arguing. I'd be the one telling everyone at the depot to pick a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same as the fast one with more breathing room. Driving lasts until about 2034. I'd be thirty-five, and I'd want to be well into a new trade before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the artic licence first, to earn more for a few years. Then around 2028 I'd start the refrigeration course part-time. I'd keep investing every month and maybe buy a small flat to rent out, if prices make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd mostly feel like I have a plan. The deadline is real, I just have time to meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the artic licence first, if driving ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it pays more now, and more money now means more saved for the change. Five or six years of better wages is worth it. I'd rather study with a bigger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd probably skip the new car I've been looking at. My old van does the job and the money's better in the fund.

say: I'd say we have **a few years** to get it right, so don't waste them.
I'd tell depot drivers to pick a **second skill**.
think: I think driving lasts until about **2034** for me.
I'd want to be well into a **new trade** before I'm thirty-five.
do: Take the **artic licence** first to earn more for a few years.
Skip the **new car** and keep investing every month.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but confident she has time to meet the deadline.
S3.quote: Five or six years of better wages is worth it. I'd rather study with a bigger cushion.
fieldNote: She **sequences** her moves: earn more first, then retrain.
She considers a **rental flat** as another source of income.
She trims small luxuries, like a **new car**, without feeling squeezed.

steps.text: Pass the articulated lorry licence and move to better-paid artic work
Start a part-time refrigeration engineering course in 2028
Skip the new car and put the money into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to retrain, and I'd mean it. I'd also say companies and governments have no excuse if people get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good. I'll probably have changed jobs twice by 2039 anyway. Having a clear date just tells me which way to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, get the artic licence and enjoy the money for a while. I'd keep investing, buy the rental flat if I can, and start retraining in my early thirties. I'd use the AI tools for everything I can at work, so I know them inside out when they take over the planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit curious about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think comes next for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something with the cold chain, maybe something I can't imagine yet. Ten years ago nobody I knew had heard of a fleet supervisor. I'm not worried about not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, the old driver I showed the AI to. He'd be sixty-eight by then, so he might just retire. The drivers I'd worry about are the ones in their forties who think ten years means never.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for anyone to retrain.
I'd say firms and governments have **no excuse** if people get left behind.
think: I think I'll have **changed jobs twice** by 2039 anyway.
A **clear date** just tells me which way to go.
do: Get the **artic licence** and enjoy the higher wages for a while.
Buy a **rental flat** if prices make sense, and keep investing.
feel: She feels **calm** and curious about what comes next.
S4.quote: The drivers I'd worry about are the ones in their forties who think ten years means never.
fieldNote: She treats a decade of warning as a **clear signpost**, not a threat.
She worries about **mid-career drivers** who may treat ten years as never.
Her plan mixes **income growth** and property, typical of her risk comfort.

steps.text: Pass the artic licence and take better-paid artic work
Buy a small flat to rent out if prices allow
Start retraining in refrigeration in her early thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of me, I'd find something, but because everybody I work with would be panicking at the same time. What would help is short, paid courses in things like refrigeration and fleet control, and companies that keep their drivers on while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd miss. I'd miss the chefs. A chef at half six in the morning with a coffee, telling me the fish was bad last week, is the best part of my job. A robot truck can't take a telling-off from a chef and laugh about it.

headlineQuote: A robot truck can't take a telling-off from a chef and laugh about it.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old chilled delivery driver** serving city restaurants for a food wholesaler.
She uses **AI every day**, has ten months saved and invests in an index fund.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing herself as the bridge to new software.
In AGI by 2028 she becomes anxious and plans **refrigeration training** during the robot gap.
With more warning she earns more first, then retrains, and **stays calm** at ten years.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, mainly because all her colleagues would panic at once.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **short, paid courses** in refrigeration and fleet control.
She wants companies to **keep drivers on** while they retrain.
